title: House Republicans Introduce Bill Seeking Three-Year Pause on H-1B Visas
excerpt: The End H-1B Visa Abuse Act of 2026, introduced by Rep. Eli Crane and backed by seven GOP cosponsors, would freeze H-1B issuance for three years, slash the annual cap, and set a $200,000 minimum wage — raising alarm among Indian tech professionals who account for over 70% of approved H-1B visas.
body:
• Rep. Eli Crane (R-AZ) introduced the End H-1B Visa Abuse Act of 2026, which would freeze all H-1B visa issuance for three years and slash the annual cap from 65,000 to 25,000 when the program resumes.
  • The bill sets a $200,000 minimum annual wage for H-1B holders, replaces the lottery with a wage-based selection system, bans third-party staffing agencies, and ends the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program.
  • Indian nationals — who received 71% of approved H-1B visas in FY 2024 — stand to be most affected, with over 1.26 million Indians already waiting in employment-based green card queues.
  • Immigration experts say the bill is unlikely to pass in its current form but signals growing political pressure on the H-1B program from multiple directions.

A group of eight Republican House members has introduced what the Immigration Accountability Project calls "the strongest H-1B bill that has ever been introduced in Congress" — legislation that would completely freeze the issuance of H-1B visas for three years and overhaul the program with sweeping restrictions when it resumes.

The End H-1B Visa Abuse Act of 2026, introduced by Rep. Eli Crane (R-AZ) on April 22, arrives amid a broader push by GOP lawmakers to curtail skilled immigration programs they argue have displaced American workers. Seven Republican cosponsors — Reps. Brian Babin (R-TX), Brandon Gill (R-TX), Paul Gosar (R-AZ), Wesley Hunt (R-TX), Tom McClintock (R-CA), Keith Self (R-TX), and Andy Ogles (R-TN) — signed on to the legislation.

"The federal government should work for hardworking citizens, not the profit margins of massive corporations. We owe it to the American people to prevent the broken H-1B system from boxing them out of jobs they are qualified to perform."

— Rep. Eli Crane (R-AZ)

What the Bill Proposes

Beyond the three-year moratorium, the bill would fundamentally reshape how the H-1B program operates. The annual visa cap would drop from 65,000 to 25,000, with existing exemptions eliminated. The lottery system would be replaced with a wage-based selection process, and employers would be required to pay H-1B workers a minimum of $200,000 per year.

Employers would need to certify they cannot find a qualified American worker and confirm they have not conducted layoffs. Third-party staffing agencies — among the largest H-1B users — would be barred from employing visa holders entirely. H-1B workers would also be prohibited from holding multiple jobs.

The legislation takes aim at several other pathways. It would end the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, ban H-1B holders from bringing dependents, and — in perhaps its most consequential provision — prohibit visa holders from adjusting their status to permanent residency, effectively severing the H-1B-to-green-card pipeline that hundreds of thousands of immigrants rely on.

Companion Legislation Adds Pressure

Rep. Chip Roy (R-TX) followed with complementary legislation, the American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act of 2026, which would cap nonimmigrant workers at 5% of any employer's U.S. workforce and allow displaced American workers to file tort claims against employers in federal court, according to Staffing Industry Analysts.

"For its nearly forty-year history, the H-1B visa has been abused, allowing employers to routinely sideline American STEM workers in favor of cheap foreign labor, while masking layoffs and wage suppression as 'shortages.'"

— Rep. Chip Roy (R-TX)

Disproportionate Impact on Indian Professionals

Indian nationals stand to be hit hardest. According to USCIS data, Indians accounted for approximately 283,000 of nearly 400,000 approved new H-1B visas in FY 2024 — 71% of the total. Over 1.26 million Indians, including dependents, are already waiting in employment-based green card queues, some facing wait times measured in decades, according to LatestLY.

A three-year freeze would mean thousands losing U.S. job opportunities, while the reduced cap and $200,000 minimum salary would sharply narrow the pipeline even after the pause ends. The elimination of OPT would cut off a critical pathway for Indian students in American universities who depend on post-graduation work authorization as a bridge to H-1B sponsorship.

Major Indian IT outsourcers have already been adjusting. TCS CEO K. Krithivasan told analysts the firm had deployed "fewer people than the number of approvals each year," calling it "part of a consistent reduction in dependency on visa-based talent over time," according to Livemint.

Prospects and Political Context

The bill arrives against a backdrop of intensifying pressure on the H-1B system. President Trump imposed a $100,000 fee on H-1B visas last September, though a federal appeals court in Boston recently refused to reinstate it after a lower court struck it down as an unlawful tax, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. The Department of Labor has initiated nearly 200 investigations into potential H-1B program abuse.

Immigration attorney Rahul Reddy, founding partner of Reddy Neumann Brown PC, called the bill "a political attack disguised as reform," noting that the $200,000 wage floor "ignores economic reality" across sectors like healthcare, education, and startups.

"The chance of this bill passing in its current form is very unlikely," Reddy wrote. "It would face major opposition from universities, hospitals, technology companies, business groups, immigration advocates, and many employers across the country."

Still, the growing number of H-1B reform proposals in the 119th Congress signals a shifting political environment around skilled immigration. For the Indian professionals whose American lives depend on these visa programs, the legislative trajectory bears close watching — even if this particular bill stalls in committee.
image_caption: House Republicans have introduced legislation seeking a three-year moratorium on new H-1B visa approvals
nri_angle: Indian nationals account for 71% of approved H-1B visas, and the bill threatens hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals and their families in the U.S. with its three-year freeze, $200,000 minimum wage, and elimination of the green card pathway.
author: Diaspora Desk
